clue.text: Have influence as a nobleman

definitions.meaning: to matter or carry weight, as in 'every vote matters'
a European aristocrat ranking roughly with a British earl

explanation.surface: Someone wields power by virtue of their aristocratic title.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to matter or carry weight; the noun is a continental title of nobility equivalent to an earl.

clue.text: Related to the ear ring on a jerk

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O
a tic is a sudden involuntary twitch or jerk

explanation.surface: An earring fixed onto an idiot's ear, punning on the anatomical sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ear ring' reads as one jewel, but 'Related to the ear' is the definition and 'ring' starts the wordplay; 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical adjective from Greek 'ous, otos', meaning of or relating to hearing anatomy.

clue.text: Hunted creatures such as beetle or cricket?

definitions.meaning: animals or birds shot or chased for sport
beetle is a dice-and-drawing pastime and cricket a bat-and-ball sport, both pastimes played to win

explanation.surface: A naturalist hunting insects like beetles and crickets.
explanation.walkthrough: The insects push you towards wildlife, but beetle is also a party pastime played with dice and cricket a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarry animals pursued in hunting share the word with contests played for amusement, of which beetle and cricket are examples.

clue.text: One beginning to parade in French city when it doesn't rain …

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: in says the opening of parade goes inside the French city

parts.note: Tours is a city on the Loire in France

indicators.note: the beginning of the word parade means its opening letter only

explanation.surface: A person begins a parade in a French city on a dry day.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition completes the proverb 'it never rains but it pours', with the ellipsis inviting the solver to finish the saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says misfortunes come all together: when there is any downpour at all, it is a deluge.

clue.text: Uninteresting place to live

definitions.meaning: dull and lacking excitement, as a monotone voice is
an apartment on one floor of a building

explanation.surface: A dull home somewhere boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull and lifeless in one sense; in British usage a self-contained apartment on a single storey in the other.

clue.text: Overtake that Cockney bloke here and there

parts.note: to overtake a car is to pass it
a Londoner's 'him' drops the H, giving 'im

explanation.surface: A driver passes a Londoner on the road at various points.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech, the working-class London accent, drops initial H, so 'him' becomes 'im.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin term used in footnotes meaning that a reference occurs throughout a text at scattered points.

clue.text: Unwelcome visitor to garden went

definitions.meaning: an unwanted plant that springs up among cultivated ones
went to the toilet, informally urinated

explanation.surface: A gardener complains about an intruder that left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went' here is the euphemism for relieving oneself, i.e. had a wee.
explanation.definitionFit: An invasive wild plant spoils flower beds; the past tense of the childish word for urinating spells the same letters.

clue.text: See 24
A penny in dole possibly making you wealthy

indicators.note: in puts the article and the penny inside the rearranged letters
possibly says the letters of dole may be arranged another way

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for an old British penny, from Latin denarius

explanation.surface: A claimant on unemployment benefit hopes a penny will make them rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dole' is British slang for unemployment benefit; 'possibly' rearranges it to LOED, and 'in' puts A and D inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for having plenty of money, rich.

clue.text: Beaten down, not beating one down

definitions.text: Beaten down, not beating one down

parts.words: Beaten down, not beating one down
parts.note: describes a boxer felled for the count, punning on beating someone down in price, which is a different thing from felling them

explanation.surface: A haggler flattened while failing to get a price reduction.
explanation.walkthrough: To beat someone down is to haggle a price lower; the phrase here means floored and unconscious instead, not someone driving a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes a fighter rendered unconscious by a blow and unable to rise before the count of ten.

clue.text: See 17
Terribly dire moments in a Chaplin film

indicators.note: terribly signals the letters of dire moments are put in a terrible jumble

explanation.surface: Frightening scenes in a silent comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1936 silent comedy by Charlie Chaplin satirising factory industrialisation.

clue.text: Encountered force in London

definitions.meaning: came across someone, past tense of 'meet'
the Metropolitan Police, London's police service, is known by this short name

explanation.surface: Someone ran into London's police.
explanation.walkthrough: The Metropolitan Police is London's police force, usually shortened in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of a verb for coming face to face; also the short name of the capital's Metropolitan Police Service.

clue.text: Piece of agricultural equipment from the US that sounds expensive

definitions.text: Piece of agricultural equipment from the US

indicators.note: that sounds says the word for costly is heard, then spelt another way

parts.note: something dear costs a lot of money

explanation.surface: An American tractor that sounds pricey.
explanation.walkthrough: John Deere is a US maker of tractors, its name pronounced like the word for costly.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractor or combine harvester is metonymically named after the American manufacturer John Deere.

clue.text: Computer scientist leaving university for Hertfordshire town

indicators.note: leaving says the university letter departs from the scientist's name

parts.note: Alan Turing, the British pioneer of computing

explanation.surface: A computer scientist quits academia to move to a commuter town.
explanation.walkthrough: Hertfordshire is a county just north of London; Tring is a small market town there.
explanation.definitionFit: A small market town in west Hertfordshire, near the Chilterns.

clue.text: Possibly a shot of Tequila that salt wouldn't go well with

definitions.meaning: a single gulp of spirits knocked back

definitions.text: that salt wouldn't go well with
definitions.meaning: a slimy garden mollusc, which salt kills

explanation.surface: A tequila shot is usually taken with salt, which the clue wittily denies.
explanation.walkthrough: Tequila is traditionally drunk with salt, so the second definition looks wrong until it becomes the garden pest that gardeners kill with salt.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulp of strong drink in one sense; a shell-less garden mollusc, which salt dehydrates, in the other.

clue.text: Singles No Angels regularly put out

indicators.note: regularly says every second letter of these words is taken

explanation.surface: Girl group No Angels releases singles at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: No Angels were a German pop group; 'put out' (release, as records) is surface-only and acts as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Single units or individual items, the number below two in plural form.

clue.text: A different aspect of disputed DNA theories

indicators.note: disputed signals that the letters of the phrase are argued over and rearranged

explanation.surface: Contested genetic hypotheses give an alternative view.
explanation.definitionFit: An alternative perspective or viewpoint on an issue.

clue.text: D results from this, within human memory

parts.note: taken as instructions, the answer says remove a short span of time (MIN, minute) from the letters MIND, which leaves just D

explanation.surface: A hint that a letter grade results from something remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay with MIN (minute) as the time, and MIND minus MIN leaves the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom refers to the span of time stretching back as far as anyone can recall, from time immemorial.

clue.text: Trim belly: about 45 inches!

indicators.note: trimming a word cuts off its first and last letters, leaving its middle

explanation.surface: A dieter's goal of trimming their waist to around forty-five inches.
explanation.walkthrough: An old English cloth measure of 45 inches; 'about' is fair because the unit varied by region.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete English measure of length for cloth, standardised at forty-five inches.

clue.text: Drug crime shows up in seaside area?

parts.note: blow is slang for cocaine
a sin is a wrongdoing or offence

explanation.surface: A drug offence turns up in a beach town.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition's whimsy: arriving casually, as the wind does off the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive unexpectedly or casually, like a breeze off the sea.

clue.text: Get a seller to service Ford model internally and make it roadworthy

indicators.note: internally says the Ford model letter goes inside the reworked letters
servicing a car means taking it apart and putting it back, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: the Model T was Henry Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: Selling a Ford after giving it a service so it passes inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to service' rearranges GET A SELLER to STREELEGAL, and 'internally' puts the Model T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes a vehicle meeting the legal requirements for being driven on public highways.

clue.text: Strange affair of basket-weaving material

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of affair are oddly rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd liaison over materials for basket weaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibre from a palm leaf, used for weaving baskets and mats.

clue.text: Administer extreme unction to a fish, say

indicators.note: say signals the phrase is spoken aloud to give a word spelt differently

parts.note: an eel is a snake-like fish

explanation.surface: A priest giving last rites to a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: An archaic verb for anointing the dying.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic verb meaning to anoint a dying person in the last rites.

clue.text: What the model artist would produce

definitions.text: What the model artist would produce

parts.words: What the model artist would produce
parts.note: an artist who is also their own model makes a picture of themselves

explanation.surface: Asks what an exemplary painter creates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model artist' looks like an ideal painter; it is a painter who sits as their own model.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture an artist paints of their own face and figure.

clue.text: Swears the blinds are missing

parts.note: the British phrase for cursing pairs two verbs; with the second (blinding) dropped, only the first, a euphemism for the F-word, remains

explanation.surface: Someone curses on finding their window blinds stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Effing and blinding' is British slang for swearing; 'blinds' looks like window coverings.
explanation.definitionFit: Uses the euphemism for the swear-word beginning with F, meaning curses.

clue.text: Dawn's brought wrong men in somehow

definitions.note: the definition reads as 'Dawn is' with the possessive serving as the verb

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are rearranged in some unspecified way

explanation.surface: Dawn complains that she has brought the wrong men in.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn looks like a woman's name; it is daybreak, and 's (is) and 'brought' link it to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak is the start of a fresh day.

clue.text: Painting interior of Gare du Nerd the wrong way round

indicators.note: the wrong way round says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Artwork inside a Paris station, with the station name deliberately mangled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' signals the hidden letters (EDUN) inside 'Gare du Nerd', a joke on Paris's Gare du Nord.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting of an unclothed figure, and the interior of the station's name reversed provides it.

clue.text: Junior featherweights eating fish?

indicators.note: eating says the words swallow the answer within them

explanation.surface: Young boxers at a lower weight are eating fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs over the end of 'Junior' into 'featherweights'.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater ornamental carp-family species, also called ide.

clue.text: Tennis player losing his footing — it's nothing to him

indicators.note: losing his footing says the player's name loses its foot, the last letter

parts.note: Rafael Nadal, the Spanish tennis champion

explanation.surface: A tennis star slips but shrugs it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' and 'to him' are links that also hint the definition is Spanish, Nadal's native tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish for zero or zilch, used informally in English.

clue.text: See 18
They don't believe find fault with a golfer

parts.note: a means one, written as the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: fault suggests the letters of find are wrong and need rearranging

parts.note: Ernie Els is a South African golfer

explanation.surface: Unbelievers criticise a golfer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find fault' reads as one phrase; 'fault' rearranges FIND plus I (from 'a', one) to INFID, and 'with' links it to the golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbelievers in a religion, people without faith.
